beginner_explanation: Peninsular rivers are those that flow across the Indian plateau. They split into two groups: those that flow west into the Arabian Sea and those that flow east into the Bay of Bengal. Important examples are the Narmada and Tapi (west) and the Godavari and Krishna (east).
intermediate_explanation: The Peninsular drainage system is older and less Himalayan-fed. West-flowing rivers like the Narmada and Tapi flow through rift valleys and are relatively short. East-flowing rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri have larger basins and support extensive agriculture. Key geographic markers include Jog Falls on the Sharavati (west-flowing), the Hirakud Dam on the Mahanadi, and Chilika Lake on the east coast, which is a haven for Olive Ridley Turtles.
advanced_explanation: The classification of Peninsular rivers into west- and east-flowing is based on the orientation of the Peninsular plateau and the direction of slope. West-flowing rivers drain into the Arabian Sea and include the Luni (which, according to the source material, is described as a tributary of the Indus River), Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati, and several smaller coastal rivers of the Western Ghats. East-flowing rivers drain into the Bay of Bengal and comprise the major river systems of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, and their tributaries. Notable features associated with these rivers are: Jog Falls (formed by the Sharavati, a west-flowing river) located in Karnataka; the Hirakud Dam, one of the longest earthen dams, built on the Mahanadi; Chilika Lake, the largest brackish water lagoon in India, situated on the Odisha coast and known for Olive Ridley Turtle nesting; and lakes such as Rolleru and Pulicat in the eastern coastal region. The source also notes that the Western Ghats (Sahyadri) are said to include the Vidhyachal, Satpura, and Aravalli ranges, and highlights geographical markers like Bhadra and Cult of Kambat in the western part of the peninsula.

subtopic: Relationship between Pressure, Air Movement, and Temperature
master_notes:
Pressure systems are defined by the relationship between surface pressure, vertical air movement, and surface temperature. According to the provided material:

• Low Pressure (L.P) is associated with air drop (descending air) at the surface, typically occurring over a cold area.
• High Pressure (H.P) is associated with air rise (ascending air) at the surface, typically occurring over a warm area.

This vertical motion drives atmospheric circulation and influences local weather conditions. A typical examination question tests this relationship directly: candidates must identify that Low Pressure corresponds to descending air over cold surfaces, while High Pressure corresponds to rising air over warm surfaces. The concept is fundamental to understanding wind formation, pressure belts, and weather systems.

⚠️ Note: The definitions provided in the source material differ from standard meteorological textbooks (where low pressure is generally associated with ascending air). This discrepancy should be verified against official NDA/CDS/AFCAT syllabus and standard NCERT geography material before final adoption.

• High Pressure (H.P) → Air rises at surface → Over warm area

subject: Geography
master_notes: The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) is a jet stream of air located above 10-12 km altitude in the upper troposphere. It is a defining feature of the Indian summer monsoon system and is directly responsible for the highest rainfall in India. The TEJ supports and strengthens the South-West (S-W) monsoon by creating upper-level divergence that enhances convective activity over the Indian subcontinent. In June, the core of the easterly jet stream shifts to flow over the southern part of the Indian peninsula, marking a critical phase in monsoon onset. Geographically, the TEJ flows east-to-west over the Indian peninsula within a pressure gradient system: a High Pressure (H.P.) zone exists over Madagascar, which is noted as a cold area compared to the warming Tibetan region, while a Low Pressure (L.P.) zone develops over the Indian landmass. This pressure contrast between the relatively cool Madagascar region and the heated Tibetan landmass drives the easterly flow of the TEJ and the overall monsoon circulation.

beginner_explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) is like a fast river of air high up in the sky, about 10-12 km above the ground. It blows from the east towards the west over India during the summer months. This jet stream is very important because it brings the heaviest rains to India during the monsoon season. In June, you can find it flowing over the southern part of India. There is high pressure (an area where air sinks and spreads out) over Madagascar, which is colder than Tibet, and low pressure (an area where air rises) over the Indian landmass. intermediate_explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) is an upper-tropospheric easterly jet stream positioned above 10-12 km altitude. It forms as part of the summer monsoon circulation over the Indian subcontinent, developing in response to the thermal contrast between the warming Tibetan region and the relatively cooler Madagascar/Mascarene High area. The TEJ is directly responsible for the highest rainfall in India and acts as a key upper-level support mechanism for the South-West monsoon. In June, the core of the jet shifts to flow over the southern part of the Indian peninsula. The High Pressure (H.P.) zone over Madagascar is noted as a cold area compared to Tibet, while the Low Pressure (L.P.) zone over the Indian landmass creates the necessary pressure gradient for the easterly flow. This pressure gradient, combined with the TEJ's upper-level divergence, enhances convective rainfall over the subcontinent.
advanced_explanation: The Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ) is a prominent upper-level atmospheric feature of the Indian summer monsoon system, situated in the upper troposphere at altitudes exceeding 10-12 km. It develops as a geostrophic response to the pronounced thermal contrast between the Tibetan Plateau, which undergoes intense surface heating during summer, and the Mascarene High region centered near Madagascar, which remains relatively cool due to oceanic influence. The TEJ flows east-to-west (easterly) and is dynamically coupled with the surface monsoon circulation through upper-level mass divergence. In June, the jet core migrates southward to flow over the southern part of the Indian peninsula, coinciding with the monsoon onset phase. The High Pressure (H.P.) zone over Madagascar represents the Mascarene High extension, which is colder than the warming Tibetan region, establishing the meridional pressure gradient that drives the TEJ. The Low Pressure (L.P.) zone over the Indian landmass corresponds to the monsoon depression system, which, through surface convergence and upper-level divergence associated with the TEJ, results in the highest rainfall in India. The TEJ also modulates the intensity and track of monsoon depressions by influencing upper-level steering flows and vertical wind shear.
